7.1: What is badness? It is what you have often seen. And whenever anything happens, keep this in mind: that it is what you have often seen. Everywhere, up and down, you will find the same things, which fill the old histories, those of the middle ages and those of our own day; which fill cities and houses now. There is nothing new: all things are both familiar and short-lived.
7.2: How can our principles become dead, unless the thoughts which correspond to them are extinguished? But it is in your power to keep fanning these thoughts into a flame. I can have the opinion I ought to have about anything. If I can, why am I disturbed? The things which are outside my mind have no relation at all to my mind.—Let this be the state of your feelings, and you stand upright. To recover your life is in your power. Look at things again as you used to look at them; for in this lies the recovery of your life.
7.3: The idle business of show, plays on the stage, flocks of sheep, herds, exercises with spears, a bone thrown to little dogs, a bit of bread tossed into fishponds, the labours of ants and their burden-carrying, the scurrying about of frightened little mice, puppets pulled by strings—all alike. It is your duty, then, in the midst of such things to show good humour and not a proud air; but to understand that every man is worth just as much as the things he busies himself about.
7.4: In conversation you must pay attention to what is said, and in every movement you must observe what is being done. And in the one you should see immediately what end it refers to, but in the other watch carefully what the thing signified is.
7.5: Is my understanding sufficient for this or not? If it is sufficient, I use it for the work as an instrument given by the universal nature. But if it is not sufficient, then either I withdraw from the work and give way to someone who can do it better, unless there is some reason why I ought not to do so; or I do it as well as I can, taking to help me the man who, with the aid of my ruling principle, can do what is now fitting and useful for the general good. For whatever I can do, either by myself or with another, ought to be directed to this alone: to what is useful and well suited to society.
7.6: How many, after being celebrated by fame, have been given up to oblivion; and how many who have celebrated the fame of others have long been dead.
7.7: Do not be ashamed to be helped; for it is your business to do your duty like a soldier in the assault on a town. What then, if you are lame and cannot climb up onto the battlements alone, but it is possible with the help of another?
7.8: Do not let future things disturb you, for you will come to them, if it must be so, carrying with you the same reason which you now use for present things.
7.9: All things are interwoven with one another, and the bond is holy; and there is hardly anything unconnected with any other thing. For things have been ordered together, and they combine to form the same universal order. For there is one universe made up of all things, and one god who pervades all things, and one substance, and one law, one common reason in all intelligent creatures, and one truth; if indeed there is also one perfection for all creatures which are of the same stock and share in reason.
7.10: Everything material soon disappears into the substance of the whole; and every formal cause is very soon taken back into the universal reason; and the memory of everything is very soon overwhelmed in time.
7.11: To the rational creature the same act is in keeping with nature and in keeping with reason.
7.12: Be upright, or be made upright.
7.13: Just as it is with the limbs in bodies which are united into one, so it is with rational beings which exist separately, for they have been made for one shared work. And you will see this more clearly if you often say to yourself that I am a member of the system of rational beings. But if, using the letter r, you say that you are a part, you do not yet love men from your heart; doing good does not yet delight you for its own sake; you still do it merely as a matter of propriety, and not yet as doing good to yourself.
7.14: Let whatever will fall from outside on the parts which can feel the effects of this fall. For those parts which have felt it will complain, if they choose. But I, unless I think that what has happened is an evil, am not harmed. And it is in my power not to think so.
7.15: Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good; just as if gold, or emerald, or purple were always saying this: Whatever anyone does or says, I must be emerald and keep my colour.
7.16: The ruling faculty does not disturb itself; I mean, it does not frighten itself or cause itself pain. But if anyone else can frighten or pain it, let him do so. For the faculty itself will not, by its own opinion, turn itself in such directions. Let the body itself take care, if it can, that it suffers nothing, and let it speak if it suffers. But the soul itself, which is subject to fear and to pain, and which has complete power to form an opinion about these things, will suffer nothing, for it will never stray into such a judgement. The ruling principle in itself needs nothing, unless it creates a need for itself; and therefore it is both free from disturbance and unhindered, if it does not disturb and hinder itself.
7.17: Eudaemonia, happiness, is a good daemon, or a good thing. What then are you doing here, O imagination? Go away, I beg you by the gods, as you came, for I do not want you. But you have come in your old way. I am not angry with you: only go away.
7.18: Is any man afraid of change? Why, what can happen without change? What, then, is more pleasing or more suitable to the universal nature? And can you take a bath unless the wood undergoes a change? And can you be nourished unless the food undergoes a change? And can anything else that is useful be done without change? Do you not see, then, that for you too to change is just the same, and equally necessary for the universal nature?
7.19: Through the universal substance, as through a raging torrent, all bodies are carried, being by their nature united with and working together with the whole, as the parts of our body do with one another. How many a Chrysippus, how many a Socrates, how many an Epictetus has time already swallowed up! And let the same thought occur to you about every man and thing.
7.20: One thing only troubles me: that I might do something which the constitution of man does not allow, or in a way which it does not allow, or which it does not allow now.
7.21: Near is your forgetting of all things; and near is the forgetting of you by all.
7.22: It is peculiar to man to love even those who do wrong. And this happens if, when they do wrong, it occurs to you that they are your kin, and that they do wrong through ignorance and unintentionally, and that soon both of you will die; and above all, that the wrongdoer has done you no harm, for he has not made your ruling faculty worse than it was before.
7.23: The universal nature, out of the universal substance, as if it were wax, now moulds a horse, and when it has broken this up, it uses the material for a tree, then for a man, then for something else; and each of these things lasts for a very short time. But it is no hardship for the vessel to be broken up, just as there was none in its being fastened together.
7.24: A scowling look is entirely unnatural; when it is often put on, the result is that all good looks die away, and at last are so completely extinguished that they cannot be lit up again at all. Try to conclude from this very fact that it is contrary to reason. For if even the awareness of doing wrong is lost, what reason is there for living any longer?
7.25: Nature, which governs the whole, will soon change all the things you see, and out of their substance will make other things, and again other things from the substance of those, so that the world may be always new.
7.26: When a man has done you any wrong, immediately consider what opinion about good or evil led him to do wrong. For when you have seen this, you will pity him, and will neither wonder nor be angry. For either you yourself think the same thing to be good that he does, or another thing of the same kind. It is your duty, then, to forgive him. But if you do not think such things to be good or evil, you will more readily be well disposed to the man who is in error.
7.27: Think not so much of what you do not have as of what you have: but of the things you have, select the best, and then reflect how eagerly they would have been sought if you did not have them. At the same time, however, take care that you do not, through being so pleased with them, get used to overvaluing them, so as to be disturbed if you should ever not have them.
7.28: Retire into yourself. The rational principle which rules has this nature: that it is content with itself when it does what is just, and so secures tranquillity.
7.29: Wipe out the imagination. Stop the pulling of the strings. Confine yourself to the present. Understand well what happens either to you or to another. Divide and separate every object into the causal, or formal, and the material. Think of your last hour. Let the wrong which is done by a man stay where the wrong was done.
7.30: Turn your attention to what is said. Let your understanding enter into the things that are being done and the things which do them.
7.31: Adorn yourself with simplicity and modesty, and with indifference towards the things which lie between virtue and vice. Love mankind. Follow God. The poet says that law rules all—and it is enough to remember that law rules all.
7.32: About death: whether it is a scattering, or a breaking up into atoms, or annihilation, it is either extinction or change.
7.33: About pain: the pain which is unbearable carries us off; but the pain which lasts a long time is bearable; and the mind keeps its own tranquillity by retiring into itself, and the ruling faculty is not made worse. But as for the parts which are harmed by pain, let them, if they can, give their opinion about it.
7.34: About fame: look at the minds of those who seek fame, observe what they are, and what kind of things they avoid, and what kind of things they pursue. And consider that, as heaps of sand piled on one another hide the earlier sands, so in life the events which go before are soon covered by those which come after.
7.35: From Plato: The man who has a lofty mind and takes a view of all time and of all substance, do you suppose it possible for him to think that human life is anything great? It is not possible, he said.—Such a man, then, will think that death also is no evil.—Certainly not.
7.36: From Antisthenes: It is royal to do good and to be spoken ill of.
7.37: It is a shameful thing for the face to be obedient, and to regulate and compose itself as the mind commands, and for the mind not to be regulated and composed by itself.
7.38: It is not right to be angry with things, For they do not care about it at all.
7.39: To the immortal gods and us give joy.
7.40:
Life must be reaped like the ripe ears of corn.
One man is born; another dies.
7.41:
If gods do not care for me and my children,
There is a reason for it.
7.42: For the good is with me, and the just.
7.43:
No joining others in their wailing,
no violent emotion.
7.44: From Plato: But I would give this man a sufficient answer, which is this: You do not speak well, if you think that a man who is good for anything at all ought to calculate the risk of life or death, and should not rather look only to this in all that he does: whether he is doing what is just or unjust, and the works of a good or a bad man.
7.45: For this is the truth of it, men of Athens: wherever a man has placed himself, thinking it the best place for him, or has been placed by a commander, there in my opinion he ought to stay and face the risk, taking nothing into account, either death or anything else, before the shame of deserting his post.
7.46: But, my good friend, consider whether what is noble and good is not something different from saving and being saved; for as to a man living for this or that length of time, at least one who is really a man, consider whether this is not a thing to be dismissed from the thoughts: and there must be no love of life; but as to these matters a man must entrust them to the Deity and believe what the women say, that no man can escape his destiny, the next question being how he may best live the time that he has to live.
7.47: Look round at the courses of the stars, as if you were moving along with them; and constantly consider the changes of the elements into one another, for such thoughts wash away the filth of life on earth.
7.48: This is a fine saying of Plato: that he who is speaking about men should also look at earthly things as if he were viewing them from some higher place; he should look at them in their assemblies, armies, farm labours, marriages, treaties, births, deaths, the noise of the law courts, desert places, various nations of barbarians, feasts, lamentations, markets, a mixture of all things and an orderly combination of opposites.
7.49: Consider the past—such great changes of political power; you may foresee also the things which will be. For they will certainly be of the same form, and it is not possible that they should stray from the order of the things which happen now; accordingly, to have contemplated human life for forty years is the same as to have contemplated it for ten thousand years. For what more will you see?
7.50:
That which has grown from the earth to the earth,
But that which has sprung from heavenly seed,
Back to the heavenly realms returns.

This is either a dissolution of the interlocking of the atoms, or a similar scattering of the unfeeling elements.
7.51:
With food and drinks and cunning magic arts
Turning the channel's course to escape from death.
The breeze which heaven has sent
We must endure, and toil without complaining.
7.52: Another may be more expert in throwing his opponent; but he is not more sociable, nor more modest, nor better disciplined to meet all that happens, nor more considerate towards the faults of his neighbours.
7.53: Where any work can be done in keeping with the reason which is common to gods and men, there we have nothing to fear; for where we are able to gain benefit by means of activity which is successful and proceeds in keeping with our constitution, there no harm is to be suspected.
7.54: Everywhere and at all times it is in your power reverently to accept your present condition, and to behave justly to those around you, and to apply your skill to your present thoughts, so that nothing slips into them without being well examined.
7.55:
Do not look around you to discover other men's ruling principles, but look straight to this: to where nature is leading you, both the universal nature through the things which happen to you, and your own nature through the acts which you must do. But every being ought to do what is in keeping with its constitution; and all other things have been made for the sake of rational beings, just as among irrational things the inferior are for the sake of the superior, but the rational for the sake of one another.

The chief principle, then, in man's constitution is the social. And the second is not to yield to the persuasions of the body—for it is the special office of the rational and intelligent movement to set limits to itself, and never to be overpowered either by the movement of the senses or by that of the appetites, for both are animal: but the intelligent movement claims superiority, and does not allow itself to be overpowered by the others. And with good reason, for it is formed by nature to use all of them. The third thing in the rational constitution is freedom from error and from deception. Let the ruling principle, then, holding fast to these things, go straight on, and it has what is its own.
7.56: Consider yourself to be dead, and to have completed your life up to the present time; and live the remainder which is allowed you in keeping with nature.
7.57: Love only what happens to you and is spun with the thread of your destiny. For what is more suitable?
7.58: In everything which happens, keep before your eyes those to whom the same things happened, and how they were annoyed, and treated them as strange things, and found fault with them: and now where are they? Nowhere. Why, then, do you too choose to act in the same way? And why do you not leave these agitations, which are foreign to nature, to those who cause them and those who are moved by them; and why are you not wholly intent on the right way of making use of the things which happen to you? For then you will use them well, and they will be material for you to work on. Only attend to yourself, and resolve to be a good man in every act you do: and remember...
7.59: Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will always bubble up, if you will always dig.
7.60: The body ought to be steady, and show no irregularity either in movement or posture. For what the mind shows in the face, by keeping in it the expression of intelligence and propriety, ought to be required also of the whole body. But all these things should be observed without affectation.
7.61: The art of life is more like wrestling than dancing, in this respect: that it should stand ready and firm to meet attacks which are sudden and unexpected.
7.62: Constantly observe who those people are whose approval you wish to have, and what ruling principles they have. For then you will neither blame those who offend involuntarily, nor will you want their approval, if you look to the sources of their opinions and appetites.
7.63: Every soul, the philosopher says, is deprived of truth against its will; so in the same way it is deprived of justice and self-control and kindness and everything of the kind. It is most necessary to bear this constantly in mind, for in this way you will be more gentle towards all.
7.64: In every pain let this thought be present: that there is no dishonour in it, nor does it make the governing intelligence worse, for it does not damage the intelligence either in so far as it is rational or in so far as it is social. Indeed, in the case of most pains let this saying of Epicurus help you: that pain is neither unbearable nor everlasting, if you bear in mind that it has its limits, and if you add nothing to it in imagination. And remember this too, that we do not notice that many things which are unpleasant to us are the same as pain, such as excessive drowsiness, and being scorched by heat, and having no appetite. When, then, you are discontented about any of these things, say to yourself that you are giving in to pain.
7.65: Take care not to feel towards the inhuman as they feel towards men.
7.66: How do we know that Telauges was not superior in character to Socrates? For it is not enough that Socrates died a nobler death, and argued more skilfully with the sophists, and spent the night in the cold with more endurance, and that when he was ordered to arrest Leon of Salamis he considered it nobler to refuse, and that he walked in a swaggering way in the streets—though as to this one may well doubt whether it was true. But we ought to inquire what kind of soul Socrates had, and whether he was able to be content with being just towards men and pious towards the gods, neither idly annoyed by men's villainy, nor making himself a slave to any man's ignorance, nor receiving as strange anything that fell to his share from the universal, nor enduring it as unbearable, nor allowing his understanding to share in the feelings of the miserable flesh.
7.67: Nature has not so mingled the intelligence with the make-up of the body as not to have allowed you the power of setting limits to yourself and of bringing under your control all that is your own; for it is very possible to be a godlike man and to be recognised as such by no one. Always bear this in mind; and another thing too, that very little indeed is needed for living a happy life. And because you have given up hope of becoming a logician and skilled in the knowledge of nature, do not for this reason give up the hope of being free and modest, and sociable and obedient to God.
7.68: It is in your power to live free from all compulsion, in the greatest tranquillity of mind, even if all the world cries out against you as much as they choose, and even if wild beasts tear to pieces the limbs of this kneaded matter which has grown around you. For what prevents the mind, in the midst of all this, from keeping itself in tranquillity and in a just judgement of all surrounding things, and in a ready use of the objects presented to it, so that the judgement may say to the thing which falls under its observation: This is what you are in reality, though in men's opinion you may appear to be of a different kind; and the use may say to what falls under the hand: You are the thing I was looking for; for to me whatever presents itself is always material for virtue, both rational and political, and in a word, for the exercise of the art which belongs to man or God. For everything which happens has a relationship either to God or to man, and is neither new nor hard to handle, but familiar and fitting material to work on.
7.69: The perfection of moral character consists in this: in living every day as if it were the last, and in being neither violently excited, nor sluggish, nor playing the hypocrite.
7.70: The gods, who are immortal, are not annoyed because for so long a time they must continually put up with men such as they are, and so many of them bad; and besides this, they also take care of them in every way. But you, who are destined to end so soon, are you tired of enduring the bad, and this too when you are one of them?
7.71: It is a ridiculous thing for a man not to flee from his own badness, which is indeed possible, but to flee from other men's badness, which is impossible.
7.72: Whatever the rational and social faculty finds to be neither intelligent nor social, it rightly judges to be inferior to itself.
7.73: When you have done a good act and another has received it, why do you still look for a third thing besides these, as fools do, either to have the reputation of having done a good act or to get something in return?
7.74: No man is tired of receiving what is useful. But it is useful to act in keeping with nature. Do not, then, be tired of receiving what is useful by doing it for others.
7.75: The nature of the All moved to make the universe. But now either everything that happens comes about by way of consequence or continuity; or even the chief things towards which the ruling power of the universe directs its own movement are governed by no rational principle. If this is remembered, it will make you more tranquil in many things.
